extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (logic/metaphysics) evaluating theories of causation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying standards for judging philosophical or scientific accounts of causation (e.g., claims about efficient causes, potential forces, volition as cause). Focuses on when a proposed antecedent legitimately counts as a cause and what evidence or reasoning is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy transfer / expenditure as a test of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the effect, or any part of the effect, to be accounted for, consists in putting matter in motion, then any of the objects present which has lost motion has contributed to the effect; and this is the true meaning of the proposition that the cause is that one of the antecedents which exerts active force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measurable expenditure or transfer of energy/motion to distinguish genuine causation from mere concomitance (Mr. Bain’s test). Example: where an effect involves motion, identify antecedents that have lost motion; treat those as causal contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reify 'potential' forces unnecessarily
rubrics_metrics.description: The force said to be stored up, and merely potential, is no more a really existing thing than any other properties of objects are really existing things. The expression is a mere artifice of language, convenient for describing the phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'stored' or 'potential' force as a property (a disposition or antecedent state) rather than as an independently existing entity. Avoid introducing new kinds of ontological stuff unless required for explanatory adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious feeling of volition is not a priori proof of universal causal type
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of energy or force, inherent in an act of will, is knowledge a priori; assurance, prior to experience, that we have the power of causing effects — this is asserted by some, but the author disputes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept subjective consciousness of effort/force as sufficient evidence that volition is an Efficient Cause for all phenomena. Examine whether the supposed a priori knowledge is actually dependent on experience and bodily mechanisms (e.g., nerves, muscles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness of antecedent and consequent does not reveal the causal connection itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The antecedent, indeed, and the consequent, are subjects of consciousness. But the connection between them is a subject of experience. I cannot admit that our consciousness of the volition contains in itself any a priori knowledge that the muscular motion will follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require empirical/experiential grounds for claiming a causal link; do not infer necessary connection from mere co-consciousness of mental states and bodily events. Note intermediate mechanisms (nerves, muscles) that mediate the relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require external/empirical evidence rather than subjective conceivability to decide between causal theories
rubrics_metrics.description: By what rule is any one to decide between one theory of this description and another? The theorists do not direct us to any external evidence; they appeal each to his own subjective feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer theories grounded in observable, intersubjective evidence. Treat appeals to what is 'natural' or 'conceivable' for an individual as unreliable for adjudicating competing causal hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralization from a single, dissimilar instance
rubrics_metrics.description: We are conscious of a single case (volition causing bodily motion). To infer that volition is the cause of every thing because it is the cause of this one particular case is unjustified; one may generalize from a single instance only when other instances resemble it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalize only from instances that share relevant similarities with the exemplar. Example: it is legitimate to ascribe life to other beings because their phenomena resemble ours; it is illegitimate to ascribe volition-as-universal-cause from the single case of our own volitions unless other phenomena show comparable markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cognitive/familiarity bias in conceivability judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a spontaneous tendency of the intellect to account for all cases of causation by assimilating them to the intentional acts of voluntary agents like itself. Conceptions are governed and limited by individual experiences and habits of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating causal theories, recognize that what seems 'natural' or 'conceivable' is heavily influenced by familiarity; correct for this bias by considering less familiar sequences and by comparing alternative explanations on empirical grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify which sense of 'cause' is being used (Aristotelian fourfold distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle enumerates four kinds of causes, viz., the Essence of a thing, the Matter of it, the Origin of Motion (Efficient Cause), and the End or Final Cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether a proposed explanation is invoking material, formal/essential, efficient, or final causes. Clarify which sense of 'cause' is intended to avoid equivocation in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invoking 'efficient causes' beyond what evidence requires (parsimony against deus ex machina / occasional causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cartesians invented the system of Occasional Causes because they could not conceive how mind and matter affect one another; they made God the mover on the occasion of the will. This is presented as an unwarranted introduction of an omnipotent agent where natural explanations can be sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not posit supernatural or ad hoc 'occasional' agents to fill explanatory gaps if natural mechanisms are plausible; reserve such moves for genuine miracles with independent justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat chance and spontaneity cautiously as explanatory causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle mentioned chance (τύχη) and spontaneity (τὸ αὐτόματον) as possible efficient causes for certain phenomena, but these were later judged inadequate for producing the ordered effects in the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that chance or spontaneity may be cited as causes for irregular phenomena, but avoid using them as satisfactory explanations for regular, law-like sequences without further specification or mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and comparative consideration as a check on claims of necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The history of science and philosophy shows divergent attitudes about the conceivability of physical causes versus volitional causes; claims that a conception is 'necessary' for all minds are undermined by historical counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about what the human mind 'must' conceive by consulting historical and cross-cultural evidence; if different thinkers have found different conceptions intelligible, be skeptical of assertions of universal cognitive constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory adequacy judged by whether the antecedent carries intrinsic reason for the consequent
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Greeks and some moderns sought causes that 'per se' carry evidence of their efficiency — that the antecedent's nature should make intelligible that it would produce the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a proposed cause contains within it, by its nature, reasons to expect the effect (mental satisfaction of intelligibility). But beware of conflating this psychological satisfaction with objective proof; require empirical corroboration.
